summary: Defines encryption transforms for ESP and IKEv2 in IPsec, based on the GOST R 34.12-2015 block ciphers Magma and Kuznyechik in Multilinear Galois Mode with external rekeying. It helps implementations wanting GOST support and does not imply IETF endorsement. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets private network tunnels use Russian standard scrambling methods.

questions: what are magma and kuznyechik ciphers
what are transform ids 32 to 35 in ikev2
subtitle: Four IPsec encryption transforms built on the Russian GOST ciphers Magma and Kuznyechik, with a tree of keys that limits how much each key is used.

tldr.problem: Implementers who want to use the Russian GOST block ciphers inside IPsec need a defined way to plug them into ESP and IKEv2.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm) transforms, IDs 32 to 35, that use the Kuznyechik or Magma cipher in Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM) with a three-level tree of keys, so that no single key protects too much data.
tldr.outcome: Two transforms give authenticated encryption for ESP and IKEv2, and two give authentication only for ESP. The RFC states that it does not imply IETF endorsement of the algorithms.

today: RFC 9227 is an Informational Independent Submission from March 2022. The unit metadata shows it is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
RFC 9227 defines four transforms for the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and IKEv2, two parts of the IPsec suite. They are based on Russian cryptographic standard algorithms, often called "GOST" algorithms, and on recommendations from the Federal Agency on Technical Regulating and Metrology (Rosstandart).

The transforms use two block ciphers from the standard GOST R 34.12-2015: Kuznyechik (128-bit block) and Magma (64-bit block). Both use a 256-bit key. They run in Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM), an authenticated encryption mode (AEAD), and they use the external rekeying mechanism of RFC 8645 to limit how often any one session key is used.

This is an Independent Submission, published for information. It was written to help implementations that wish to support the GOST algorithms and does not imply IETF endorsement of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some countries have their own official secret-code methods. This document explains how to use two of them inside secure network tunnels.

sections.title: The Four Transforms
sections.content:
All four are Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm) transforms and all use MGM with tree-based external rekeying. They differ in the cipher and in what they provide.

  • ENCR_KUZNYECHIK_MGM_KTREE (ID 32) and ENCR_MAGMA_MGM_KTREE (ID 33) give confidentiality and message authentication, so they can be used in both ESP and IKEv2.
  • ENCR_KUZNYECHIK_MGM_MAC_KTREE (ID 34) and ENCR_MAGMA_MGM_MAC_KTREE (ID 35) give no confidentiality and can only be used in ESP, not IKEv2.

The MAC-only transforms are still defined as Type 1 transforms because they must carry an Initialization Vector (IV), which Type 3 (Integrity Algorithm) transforms cannot do.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four flavors: two that both scramble and sign the message, and two that only sign it, so you can tell nobody changed it.

sections.title: Tree-Based Rekeying and Keying Material
sections.content:
The key given to the transform is never used directly on messages. It is the root of a tree of keys, and a leaf key K_msg protects the messages. The tree has three levels and uses the KDF_GOSTR3411_2012_256 key derivation function from RFC 7836, with the labels level1, level2 and level3.

The parameters i1 (one octet) and i2, i3 (two octets each) pick the leaf. That allows up to 2^8 keys on level 1 and 2^16 on levels 2 and 3, so 2^40 possible leaf keys per Security Association. The RFC places no requirement on how often rekeying happens; the sender follows its own policy.

The transform key is the tree root plus a secret salt. For the Kuznyechik transforms it is 352 bits (a 256-bit root key and a 96-bit salt). For the Magma transforms it is 288 bits (a 256-bit root key and a 32-bit salt). In ESP the key comes from KEYMAT, and in IKEv2 it is SK_ei or SK_er. The IKEv2 keys SK_ai and SK_ar are not used and MUST be treated as zero length.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one key locking everything, there is a big family tree of keys. Each small batch of messages gets its own key from the bottom of the tree.

sections.title: IV, Nonce, Tag and AAD
sections.content:
Every protected message MUST carry a 64-bit IV made of i1, i2, i3 and a 3-octet counter pnum. Up to 2^24 messages may be protected with one leaf key. The IV MUST NOT be used more than once for a given SA, but it need not be unpredictable.

MGM also needs a nonce. It is built from a zero octet, the 24-bit pnum and the secret salt, which is fixed for the SA and never sent on the wire: 12 octets of salt for Kuznyechik and 4 octets for Magma. The integrity check value is 96 bits for Kuznyechik and 64 bits (the full block) for Magma. No plaintext padding is added beyond what the protocol itself needs.

The additional authenticated data (AAD) for the encrypting transforms in ESP is the SPI and the (extended) sequence number. For the MAC-only transforms it also includes the IV and the part of the packet that would normally be encrypted. In IKEv2 it covers the IKE header, any unencrypted payloads and the Encrypted payload header or Encrypted Fragment payload header.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a little label saying which key from the tree was used and which message number it is, so the receiver can find the right key.

sections.title: Using the Transforms
sections.content:
When the SA starts, the sender sets i1, i2 and i3 to 0 and computes a leaf key, with pnum starting at 0. To change the leaf, the sender increments i3 and resets pnum to 0. When an i3 key has been used enough, it increments i2 and resets i3, and a similar step handles i1.

A combination of i1, i2, i3 and pnum MUST NOT repeat for an SA, so counters may not wrap. If all four reach their maximum, the IPsec SA becomes unusable. The sender SHOULD also count octets per leaf key and switch keys at the latest at the limits in the security section.

The receiver always uses i1, i2 and i3 from the received message and computes a new leaf key when they change. It may cache recent leaf keys and keep an old one for a while in case packets arrive out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender hands out keys one after another and never reuses a number. The receiver just reads the label on each message to find the matching key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MGM breaks if a nonce repeats for a key, so these transforms MUST NOT be used with manual keying. Using one key for too much data helps attackers, which matters most for a 64-bit block cipher like Magma. The rekeying tree is the RFC's mitigation for that weakness.

The recommended limit per K_msg is 2^41 octets for the Kuznyechik transforms and 2^28 octets for the Magma transforms. The Kuznyechik limit cannot be reached, because the design caps a leaf key at 2^24 messages of at most 2^16 octets each, or 2^40 octets.

An attacker can send packets with arbitrary i1, i2 and i3 values. That forces the receiver to compute leaf keys, which uses CPU, and to attempt failing verifications. Implementations MAY start rekeying if they see too many packets with an invalid ICV.
sections.plainLanguage: A key that is used too many times gets weak, like a pencil worn down to a stub. Switching keys often keeps every key fresh.
